utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can follow it in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Denise Gustin and I would like to introduce Dominic Raab who is the legal adviser to the British Embassy in The Hague who will be here at least for the beginning of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you and welcome, Mr. Raab. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. I hear that you have already been communicated some good news by our president, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had a call about 10.00 last night from the U.S. Embassy saying that the general licence had been issued. They didn't have it in their hands but they had word from Washington that it was issued so I'm satisfied that that's happened and I spoke with the President this morning and he confirmed that, so I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I that's done. May I raise one matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's unless the Prosecution has matters to raise before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, there was discussion regarding the statement of a potential witness and the Court ordered that it be turned over in redacted form. Your Honour, I've received it and had a look and it and it appears to me -- and of course it's almost impossible for me to tell, but it appears to me the redactions are really, really excessive and that it has been redacted to the point where it basically does not make sense. And so what I would request is that Your Honours review those redactions, because it's basically -- if the purpose was to advise the Defence as to what this witness was prepared to say, I think it has failed because of the excessive redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I speak for myself. I haven't seen the redacted form and I haven't read the unredacted statement for a very simple reason that I wanted to hear your reaction first before going through this statement, because it would have made much more sense then than if I had read it first and then listened to what you had to say based on a redacted form. So I need to first make comparative exercise between the two texts and then we will come back to it probably I come back to it tomorrow. You'll be here tomorrow morning, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and I want to underscore the objection that I believe was made by Ms. Baruch yesterday and that is that we sort of have a fundamental objection to the Prosecution asking the Court to turn a Prosecution witness into a Court witness because we just think that's not proper. And I think that's a good objection, frankly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Any further matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. All right. The witness is in open session, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is one area where we will need to go into private to deal with some issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Usher, could you bring the witness in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're familiar with this Tribunal so we don't need any elaborate introductions. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration you're required to make before you start giving evidence. Please proceed and that will be your sol up undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir, please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has sometime back provided us with your statement as an expert witness pursuant to Rule 94 bis which we have gone through. Today, and part of tomorrow, you're going to be examined-in-chief by Mr. Nicholls, based mainly on your report. Cross-examination is being deferred to sometime in October, unless we agree that it will take place late August but that depends on some arrangements that may need to be made and also on whether Mr. Ackerman will be prepared to cross-examine you late August. But in any case, the message is that you are only going to be examined in chief now and that cross-examination is deferred. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: My name is Ewan Brown. I was born on the 15th of May, 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know that you've testified previously in this Tribunal but I'd like to remind you that because we both speak the same language and because our conversation is being translated, we need to allow a little bit of a gap between questions and answers. Could you state your citizenship, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm a British citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where are you -- what is your current employment?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm currently an analyst working in the military analysis team at the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I arrived here in August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We are in open session, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'd like to now ask you a few questions about how you came to be asked to write this report and what you did in the process of preparing the report. Have you brought a copy of your report with you today?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, your report entitled Military Developments in the Bosanska Krajina 1992: A Background Study, dated 27 November, 2002, could you tell the Court first of all, please, who asked you to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked me to prepare the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what direction did she give you? What -- was this a written memo asking you to prepare the report or a conversation? Can you describe what you were told when you were asked to prepare this report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: There wasn't a written memo in relation to the preparation of the report. Ms. Korner simply asked me to provide a background analysis report on the activity of the JNA, and the VRS, and Bosnian Serb forces working in the Krajina in 1992. It was a somewhat general tasking from her and I received that tasking around the middle of 2000. I believe around May or June, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you used mainly or exclusively documentary material in this report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that your decision or the decision of anybody else?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It was my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you briefly go through which types of documentary material, what sources of information you relied upon in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: When I was asked to compile the report, I'd already been doing some work in exploiting the first military -- the 1st Krajina Corps military collection which had been seized by the Office of the Prosecutor sometime prior to this. And I utilised a significant number of documents from that military collection which were the archive or a component of the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps. I also utilised other military documents which had arrived in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, as well as police reports which specifically made reference to military issues or joint operations. I utilised a number of political documents, documents written by political bodies or decisions from political bodies where I felt that there was a defence-related issue or military-related issue or it reflected on some of the other military documents and I also used a small number of open-source documents, media references and one or two videos, I believe. So in essence, the documentation can be split into four sections, military documents, a number of police documents, some political documents, and some open-source material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who selected the documents to be included in the report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this report is quite lengthy, just about 200 pages, and it's got almost or over 900 footnotes and citations. Approximately how many documents did you use in the report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm unclear exactly the number. I think it maybe around about over 600. There are a number of duplications and multiple references, same document being referenced a number of times in the footnotes but I'm unclear exactly how many documents but there are over 900 references, footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One of the -- right in the beginning of your report in the introduction, you state what the aim of the report was. Could you explain to the Tribunal what you - what your aim was in writing this report, what you hoped to achieve in writing it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think the aim is on page 4 in the introduction is simply to provide a background analysis from documentary material on the activities of the JNA, VRS, and other military forces operating in Northern Bosnia known as the Krajina -- Bosnian Krajina in 1992. What I wanted to try and do was to break that down into various themes that I believe might be relevant to that aim of understanding some or getting a better analysis or understanding of the military activity in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that aim and the themes you just talked about, again, was that your decision to structure the report that way or was that -- did anybody else tell you to write the report in that manner?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The aim of course was really given by Ms. Korner but in terms of the structure of the report, the content of the report, and the way that I decided to write it, then that was purely my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also in your report say that the report has some limitations, as obviously any report does. Could you describe to the Chamber what you believe any limitations of your report may be.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I think it is important to note that the document does have some limitations. It's not an exhaustive study of every aspect of military operations in the Krajina. I think I would be here until -- well, for a long time if I had to do that. So there is a limitation, a practical limitation on it that I was set. It does cover predominantly 1992 so that a time limitation there, doesn't necessarily go into significant detail and activities in 1991 or necessarily activities post-1992 so there is a time limitation there too. And it is a documentary-based report. That in itself has a potential limiting factor too. These are some of the limitations. The main one I would argue though is that it does not cover every single aspect of activities in the Krajina and it is focused heavily on the activities of the Bosnian Serb forces. So I would ask you to be wary of those limitations in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I would like to now tender the report, Your Honours, which will be P2416, I believe. There is also an errata sheet to the report which Mr. Brown has prepared, which I suppose could be P2416.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while I'm here, Mr. Brown, can you just tell us what that errata sheet is and why you prepared that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Obviously it's a rather lengthy report and it was written over a reasonable period of time and on looking at it again, there are a number of errors in it, in terms of spelling mistakes, ERN references which were either wrong or subsequent translations came out, maybe I quoted the draft translation. And a number of -- a few, very few, changes in terms of translation. I may have quoted a draft translation and when it came back in final, the translation was slightly different. So it's not substantive changes particularly but small typing errors and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to now begin discussing your report, moving to the first section. You begin section 1, Political/Military Developments on page 12 of the report, and the first portion of the executive summary of the report on page 5 also deals with these developments. In essence, you've begun your report here by talking about, I suppose, a shift or changes in the policy of the JNA, and you wrote in your executive summary that: "By April, 1992, there had been a growing convergence between the JNA and the Serbian Democratic Party or SDS." Can you explain why you began the report on this issue.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: When I came to write the report, I wanted to try and put some contextual background to the activities of the JNA earlier in 1992, and I looked at JNA military documents from the period in essence to try and lay some kind of framework or groundwork on what the JNA's perspective was on the issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to looking at issues in relation to the 5th Corps and its activities, 5th Corps, 1st Krajina Corps and its activities later in 1992. So it really was an attempt as an introduction to lay some context from what the documents told me in the early part of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at your report, in paragraph 1.3, on page 12, the first document you selected to footnote is a report on the state of combat readiness for 1991 of the 2nd Military District command. That has ERN number 0110-9699 for the translation. Can you tell us why you selected that document and what that says to you on this topic we have been talking about, the background of the problems facing the JNA and the 5th Corps at this time period?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This is a document which from the title is somewhat self explanatory and it's from the 2nd military district which had just recently been established as a result in part of the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia and it's a report in early January from the 2nd military district, doing I would argue two things. One is looking back to some degree on the activities in 1991 in Croatia and the formation of the 2nd Military District and the problems or otherwise from that deployment, but also looking towards Bosnia-Herzegovina and the problems that they were highlighting as potential difficulties for the district. The 2nd Military District was headquartered in Sarajevo and covered, to all intents and purposes, the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was a document both looking back into 1991 as well as looking at some of the issues and problems that they believed they were going to be facing in the district in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in relation to the second part, and reading this document, it is clear that they were very aware of the problems of ethnic division and the problems that ethnic or they call them mono national parties had caused in Bosnia-Herzegovina and they are wary or critical of all three ethnic parties in this document, and that the problems are going to occur in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you state in your executive summary, concerning this section, that: "At this time the JNA adopted a twin-track policy of attempting to reduce tensions in order to keep the republic within the federal Yugoslavia, yet at the same time provide support to Bosnian Serbs." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that is the case and I would argue that's what the documents would appear to indicate. The JNA of course was a federal body and it would seem possibly somewhat self-evident that it would wish to try and maintain Yugoslavia as an entity despite Croatia and Slovenia seceding from Yugoslavia. There are also references in the early part of 1992 and in fact going into the spring of 1992 where the JNA was saying that it was trying to stop ethnic divisions and ethnic tensions and reduce ethnic tensions in areas, but I would believe that from those it was as part of trying to keep Bosnia within Yugoslavia. It's evident that as we move into the spring of 1992, that it's clear that they were, however, providing assistance to the Bosnian Serbs and that there was this growing convergence between the JNA and the SDS in Bosnia in particular, and manifested itself in May 1992 with the establishment of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Your Honours. It has not previously been an exhibit. We are up to P2417. Your Honours, we are using Sanction for this presentation. I've just been told that we will tender hard copies at the end of these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, on the same topic, you -- I'd like to look at the second document which you selected for inclusion in your report. It's footnote 2. Again, another report, this one titled: "Based on Assessments of the Situation in the Territory of BH in the Area of Responsibility of the 2nd Military District." This has been previously exhibited as P1574. Briefly, can you tell us why you included this document as well and if there are any areas you'd like to highlight which go to what we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This is also a document from the headquarters of the 2nd Military District and I thought it was of note to compare some of the language and content of this document with the one previously which was written only two months prior to that. The first document in January is also critical at times of the Bosnian Serbs and is critical in general of all ethnic parties as contributing to -- they use the word chaos in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This document in March, 1992, written by the -- certainly signed off by the commander of the 2nd Military District, I would argue indicates this shift. There are references here to the SDS arming or providing arms, there are references to the commander saying that the position of the Serbs is the most -- the Bosnian Serbs, the SDS is the most appropriate and that they will be meeting with the leaders of the Serbian people and these specifically makes reference to Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, and Djukic, the key republican or key Bosnian Serb leadership at the time. And I think when you compare the two documents, you do see this gradual shift or this notable shift in a relatively short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on and look quickly at another document. This is number 6 in your footnotes. This has been previously exhibited as P1576. And it's actually earlier. It's from the December 1991. It's entitled: "Directive on the Use of the Armed Forces for the Preparation and Performance of Combat Operations in the Forthcoming Period." You cite this in paragraph 1.7 of your report. And you state that: "During the latter stages of the operations in Croatia, the JNA's own directive had declared that THE objective of the JNA was the protection of the Serbian population," and I believe that appears on page 3 of the document. I think this is fairly self-evident, but can you explain why you selected this document and its significance.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think in -- as you say, it's somewhat self-evident in terms of what it says, that its aims are to protect the Serbian population. I would also stress that it does mention that an aim is also for the peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis and the creation of conditions in which Yugoslavia may be preserved for those people who wish to live in it. This I believe highlights this position of trying to maintain Yugoslavia or at least as much of Yugoslavia as can be maintained, as well as a specific reference to the Serbian people. It doesn't talk about all peoples but the protection -- protection of all peoples but specifically the Serbian people. I would to some extent caution this document in that it is making reference to operations in Croatia. It's a directive that came out in December 1991. I think it's an important document as well in that there was a directive in September 1991 from the JNA which dealt with launching operations into Croatia, and the aim of those operations were notably far more -- far grander, if you like, to head to the Hungarian border to deblock barracks and by the 10th of December, 1991, those JNA objectives had become far more restricted to those in essence protecting the Serb areas and maintaining as much of Yugoslavia as possible. So I think this is a document that predominantly refers to Croatia but it is from the senior JNA leadership and I believe that that directive was also the type of directives that we see or the instructions that we see occurring in the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear. A similar document I'd like to talk about next, this is footnoted 21, previously exhibited as P365. And you reference this in paragraph 1.18 of your report, which is on page 17. This is a letter to the Banja Luka Corps from the 5th Corps command and again, you've spoken about in your report that this document is an example of the growing emphasis on protection of the Serbian population. Could you please just take a look at this document, refresh yourself, and tell us why this one was significant to you and you included it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think there are a number of interesting strands in this document from General Talic written on the 3rd of April. It articulates or looks back to what the 5th Corps had achieved or what he believed the 5th Corps had achieved in its operations so far and I draw your attention to the section halfway down the page where he states that: "By their eight-month struggle, the soldiers of the 5th Corps had saved the Serbian people of Western Slavonia from being exterminated by the Ustashas. We had liberated and captured Serbian territories in this part of Croatia, prevented the penetration of Paraga troopers, which are Croatian nationalists, in the territory of the Bosnian Krajina and created conditions for the arrival of the UN peacekeeping forces which would mark the end of the war in these parts." By specifically referencing in essence protecting the Serbian people and extermination of the Serbian people in those areas, I think it's an useful indicator of his belief at the time. I'd also draw your attention to the issue in relation to the barricades in Banja Luka on the 3rd of April, where he clearly was aware of the fact that SOS or Serbian armed forces had set up barricades, and he himself said that they represented a peace -- a threat to the peace in the Bosnian Krajina. But he also qualifies that by saying that there was no real reason for this because the demands that had been set by this group could have and must be resolved peacefully. So he is in essence articulating that this Serbian armed group should be negotiated with and their issues and demands be resolved peacefully. The last paragraph, paragraph 3, states that: "Make sure the Banja Luka Corps remains a reliable defenders of all peoples and nationalities in the Bosnian Krajina and it enables the people of the Krajina to peacefully build a democratic government and build together with other peoples and republics that wish to do so a new common state in which our children will not fight wars." Now, on the face of it that seems a reasonable statement but the fact that he appears to be talking about building a new common state with other republics I would argue again is indicative of this desire at this time to try and maintain Yugoslavia as a viable entity and to keep Bosnia or as much of Bosnia in one state. So I think there are a few interesting strands in this document from Talic in early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you as well, because obviously we won't be able to go through all of the military documents which you've cited in your report, but the language here which we see, about how: "The 5th Corps saved the Serbian peoples of Western Slavonia from being exterminated by Ustashas," did that type of language, the tenor we see there, did that increase, decrease, or stay the same, this sort of I'd call it inflammatory, aggressive language, during the period we are talking about in the documents which you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It definitely increased from this period and I've made reference to that later on in the report, in press reports, documents, General Talic's own documents, that type of language certainly increased through 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. There is only one other document I'd like to look at with you while we are on this topic before we move on, and that is the document cited in footnote 49. This is a 30th division, 30th Partisan division command order from April 1992. It has previously been exhibited as P888. And you cite that in paragraph 1.37 of your report on page 23. And this document in April, on page 1, states: "Re-examine the officer structure of the battalion and if possible assign reserve officers to appropriate positions regardless of whether they are members of the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party, or not." Can you tell us if you see any significance of that statement or other statements in this document, regarding the topic we are talking about, the growing convergence of the JNA to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I only thought it was of value in placing that in some contrast with the early January 1992 document from the 2nd Military District which did, on the face of it, criticise the SDS and criticised the three ethnic parties as being a contributing factor to the chaos in Bosnia. And here we have a few months later the 30th division, which was a subordinate formation of the 5th Corps saying that in essence, we will have SDS officers in the division. It doesn't specifically make reference to any other party but I thought that was of some interest in contrasting with some of the earlier references.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you go to page 4 of this document, Mr. Brown --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could look at page 4 of the same document, Mr. Brown, at the top of the page paragraph D, Show of Force is the heading of that paragraph. The document states: "Put on a show of force by moving units and combat hardware, particularly towards municipalities of Jajce and Bugojno and in certain situations also towards Kljuc municipality, in order to defuse tensions and prevent interethnic clashes in the area where Serbs are a minority." We've seen -- we've talked about similar references. Could you explain that portion?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, again, here, I would argue this comment would appear to show this convergence that the JNA, which at this time was -- this convergence in essence with the protecting the Serbian interests and Serbian people, and here we show the 30th division basically putting on a show of force in two municipalities which were predominantly non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, if you could look at page 5 of this document, the last page, paragraph 7, Command and Control, you cited this in your report on page 23, paragraph 1.37, and you talked about the -- part of this order which states: "In the areas of responsibility of all units, intensify cooperation with SJB and TO organs and ensure ongoing and secure communications with them." Can you tell us what the significance was at all about this intensified cooperation which appears in this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This is one of a number of documents around this time which indicate or instruct that type of cooperation and I think it's a mechanism by which -- to ensure better coordination, better control, in the areas that the division is going to be working in, and it becomes a feature regularly and is referenced regularly in military documents throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I misspoke. It wasn't this precise document which was cited for that proposition, but it's the same point. If we can move along to another topic now, it's related. We have been talking about the convergence of the JNA and the SDS, and I think you said right at the beginning that the greatest manifestation of that was the creation of the VRS; is that right? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to talk now about that period. You stated in your executive summary the months of April and May 1992 you saw the cementing of links between the SDS and the 5th Corps; the announcement of the goals of the Bosnian Serbs; the transition of the JNA into the army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the VRS; and the start of military operations in the Bosanska Krajina. And that's what I'd like to talk about now, those topics. On page 24 of your report, you have an entire section devoted to the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Hercegovina. We will talk about that meeting in some detail but can you tell us why you felt that that needed to be included and why it was such an important event in the military history of 1992 in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: When I was looking at details in relation to the establishment of the army of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina later known as the VRS, I had to look at this document because that is when the establishment instruction was passed. And although in no ways was the 16th assembly session, if you like, the start point of political process, it seemed to be from the minutes of this meeting, an absolutely crucial -- a crucial meeting, and to some extent the culmination of a political process that had started some time ago, some time previous to that. Importantly, it seemed to be that point of convergence whereby the VRS was established from the JNA and the strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serbs were announced, and in essence the war objectives of the Bosnian Serbs was announced and the army was created. And it just seemed a particularly significant meeting with particularly significant decisions taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This document has been discussed before so we won't go through every aspect of it but let's look at the actual minutes of the 16th assembly session. That was previously exhibited as P50, I believe. It's also footnote 50 in your report. In paragraph 1.40 of your report, on page 24, you list the six strategic goals and state that: "Karadzic placed these strategic goals in hierarchical order." You go on to say, this is on page 25 at the top: "Subsequent Serb military operations can be linked to these articulated goals, and in the context of the military, these strategic goals gave them a clearly identified set of objectives from which they were to develop operational and tactical planning." And in the next sentence, you continue, these articulated goals were in essence a plan to seize and control territory, establish the Serb republic, defend defined borders, separate -- and separate the ethnic groups within Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you explain that, please, how these six strategic goals are related to concrete military operations and objectives?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The -- there are a number of very clear examples in specific terms to the strategic goals which you can show direct military action. If you take, for example, strategic goal number 2 which the establishment of a corridor link, which Karadzic said was important not only to link the Serbian areas within Bosnia but it was also important to link the Serbian areas in Croatia and those two areas with Yugoslavia, within a matter of weeks, the 1st Krajina Corps were launching Operation Corridor 92 and very successfully managed to secure a corridor link which was expanded through the summer of 1992 and never severed in the war. That is a very visible, to me, a visible indicator that the strategic goals were not simply interesting and rarefy political discussions, but that military action fell from the announcement of these political goals and I would argue in other areas that you can show that. One of them relates to an establishment of a border on the Una and Neretva rivers and operations in May and June included operations in the Una -- around the Una river area in Bosanski Novi and Bosanska Krupa and the likes. So I would argue that those two very visible examples show that there were -- there was significant importance in these goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, it just occurs to me, having read this report and following the trail that both questions and answers are following, that there are some areas where you would obviously come forward with a strong contestation and other areas where probably you would not. If at any time in the course of the questions and answers there are areas which you don't intend to contest or that you agree with, perhaps you could indicate those to us and we can proceed quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll see what I can do to accommodate you, Your Honour. I'll think about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Another portion of your report, you state that the first strategic goal, separation from the other two national communities was first in hierarchical order and was considered the most important goal. Can you tell us how you arrived at that, why you say that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It was stated by Mr. Krajisnik in the report that that was the most important goal and he was also, according to him and the minutes, involved in the production of these goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you also conclude or state in your report that this first strategic goal was necessarily really about resettlement. Can we talk about that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think there are a number of significant references in the minutes from both the senior leadership and also from the delegates and also from General Mladic that would indicate that strategic goal number 1 was not simply about separating Bosnia but that it would involve -- or this process of separation would involve the resettlement, and it's a word they themselves use or a number of occasions, that that would involve the movement out or resettlement of a significant number of people from the RS territory, and I can go through some of those just to highlight that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: When Mr. Karadzic discussed initially the strategic goals he said in relation to the strategic goal number 1 that the first goal is separation from the other two national communities, separation of states but he goes on to say that, "it's separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially this century to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state." So this is an early indication that this is already calling them their enemies. He later goes on to say himself, on page 16 of the translation, that, "we don't want to get a state in which a huge number of those who are against that -- which includes a huge number of those who are against that state." And then there are a number of statements by delegates later on which openly discuss the issue of resettlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we are, or you are, referring always all the time to the minutes of the 16th session, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I knew that but for the record I wanted it to be said, to be stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And then as Mr. Brown said, the first statement, "we do not want to get a state which has a huge number of those who are against that state," is on page 16. There is a similar reference, if we could look at that briefly, on page 20, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, once Dr. Karadzic made his speech the various delegates took turns in speaking too and one of the delegates Trifko Radic, said, "I've heard reports on how it was when the Swedes and Norwegians were separating. The process of resettlement lasted ten years, we will see the same thing here but it is still better to do that and know exactly who is resettling where. It is going to be a difficult process. It will require a lot of toil and effort and explanation to the people who will have to leave their hearths. That is why you gentlemen, high up in the government and the Presidency, will be working on this with our TV network and preparing the people psychologically that on one -- that one day this will have to happen."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is something wrong with the reference. Mr. Nicholls said it was on page 20 but there is nothing on page 20 about Trifko Radic. Page 20 is still Karadzic speaking, so the page number is apparently wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at page 19, Mr. Ackerman, in the version we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My page 19 is still Karadzic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, for the record we need to check this reference by direct reference to the document itself, which I don't have in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just say for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime you may proceed. I've taken note of your remark and objection, Mr. Ackerman, and I will act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have found Trifko Radic begins speaking on page 28 for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Document I have doesn't have an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can move on, I can say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can move on. I mean, it's -- if the page number or reference to the page number is wrong, then we will have it corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this is a huge problem if I'm going to be preparing a cross-examination based on a different document than the witness was using.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think it will be a huge problem because fortunately he's going to have around two months to prepare. He's going to have a transcript before he prepares and if he doesn't have this version which I think he does have, of the minutes, we can provide him with them. While we are going through this, I hope he's able, Mr. Ackerman is able to follow what we are doing on the screen in front of him. For instance, here we have page 19, Mr. Krajisnik saying, "Here we have Trifko Radic asking for the floor. Trifko Radic:" And he begins to speak. I don't think this is going to be anything which is difficult for Mr. Ackerman to deal with in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The concern I have is this. Let me be a little more specific. What I'm looking at here is what I believe to be in the record as Exhibit P50, and if what we are referring to is Exhibit P50, and the Prosecution is referring to something else that's not in the record as Exhibit P50 then we have a problem and if what I'm looking at here is not P50, which is what the indication I have is, then I have a problem. But somewhere this needs to get straightened out and if we could look at Exhibit P50 that's in the record, we would know whether it's what I'm looking at or what Mr. Nicholls is looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could I have Exhibit P50 in the English language, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is disclosure 2.21 if that helps Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the disclosure number on the document I'm looking at, Your Honour, 2.21.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents in B/C/S and English do not match. They are two different pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you heard the comment, the remark? It's definitely -- the document that we have in our records, Mr. Ackerman, which is Exhibit P50, the English version, that's A, starting with ERN number 00913501, page 19, it's Mr. Trifko Radic who starts making a speech, and that's after being introduced by Krajisnik. And on page 20, as indeed we find in the witness's report, second paragraph, we find exactly the words that have been reproduced in the report. So for the record, and for the purposes of your cross-examination, this is what we have and this is what you have to refer to. If you have another document which on page 20 and on page 19 does not purport to reproduce the speech of Mr. Radic, then tell me and I will have it substituted for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's fairly obvious that I do not have the most recent translation, since I don't have any ERN numbers on my documents or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But can you -- I think you have stated in the past that if we give you the ERN number, you can locate it in your database?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I tried to. I don't have it. I don't have that ERN number in my database so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin, do you have a spare copy of P50 or can we make a photocopy of P50 now and have it handed to Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's displayed on the ELMO. That's the whole points of the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the point. I would prefer to proceed and put Mr. Ackerman's mind at rest, that he has the document readily available. Usher, can I ask you to be kind enough to photocopy this document for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd just like to say, Your Honour, I'm told by Ms. Gustin that the copy which we are all using was disclosed to Mr. Ackerman on the 8th of March, 2001. I've lost about ten minutes here, in the limited amount of time I have, with this witness who I consider important, who has written a 200 page document. I have sympathy if he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right let's proceed, Mr. Nicholls, because you are losing further time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just understand. I would prefer there not be objections and time wasted if he doesn't have a document here which we have disclosed to him because he's not going to have to stand up tomorrow morning and deal with this. He can find the documents later. He has the transcript and if he has to match ERN numbers, I don't think it's our problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Brown. I'll try to come back to where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In any event, let's move on to another reference here, which I believe shows that some of these processes discussed in the strategic goals had already begun and I'm thinking about page 25 of the document which we have before us, that's for the record 00913525, which I have as a person from Bosanska Krupa, Miroslav Vjestica, speaking. Could you find that entry, please?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I don't think - I may be wrong - that you specifically cited this entry but could you tell us what significance this has to you? I'm thinking as most importantly about the bottom section of the page.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vjestica gives an overview of what happened in Bosanska Krupa and I'll draw your attention to some sections of this which I also think are relevant to the issue of resettlement and the awareness that this was going to be a feature. Some of the sections halfway down, "what have we done in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa? I must tell you to remind you all that Serbs comprise only 24 per cent of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. There are 14 and a half thousand of us and there are 47.000 Muslims. As our president has said, we in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa did not want war but we were forced into it." Later on, he says, "for a year and a half we have been preparing for war in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa because we know that there will be war and that it would -- that it could not be avoided." And at the bottom he says, "What are our adversaries doing? At the moment they are all in the Cazin Krajina on the right bank of the Una river. There are no more Muslims in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All the enclaves that were there, Rapusa, Veliki, Vrbovik, Ostrojnica, Babic, Muslim Jasenica, and Zavir, we have evacuated them so that there will be none there for the duration of the war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it's unlikely after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the river -- that the right bank of the Una River was the border."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: There are a couple of other sections in Mr. Vjestica's speech that I would draw your attention to, bearing in mind for a little bit later. He talks about all minutes of the SDA executive board, SDA party, regional board meetings, since a person from Bosanska Krupa was the President - this is, sorry, on page 26 - "having captured all their documentation on their Territorial Defence units and their Crisis Staffs we know that at the moment they do not have any weapons, not as much as they need right now. They do not have ammunition or equipment, they do not have, in other words, a tank." He also talked about what was happening in his neighbouring municipalities, the municipality in particular Bosanski Novi. I draw your attention to what he says about that because I believe that that is a bearing later on. "As for Bosanski Novi, let me tell you that I was there yesterday. Bosanski Novi is sealed off. An ultimatum has been issued and a deadline settled for the Muslims to surrender their weapons. Some of them have, some of them have not. Yesterday there was shooting. What will happen today, I believe, they will surrender. The same is going on in Sanski Most. I think the Muslims will be disarmed there too." The day previous in Bosanski Novi, there had been an attack and there is some documentation later on which I will draw your attention to but I would like you to be aware of his comments in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear before we move on, that segment is also on page 26. Was the attack, which we will talk about later in Bosanski Novi, was that related to the issue here spoken about of disarmament, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The other part of this I'd like you to discuss, briefly, is all throughout this meeting, there is discussion about a war option or whether or not, and the scope of any coming war, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think many of the delegates talk about that and make direct reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On page 22, which is ERN number 00913522, Mr. Dragan Kalinic speaks, and can you briefly give us your interpretation of his statement, which appears in the second paragraph where he talks about have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation, and then begins to advocate for the war option?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kalinic gave a rather aggressive speech. Mr. Kalinic was also at this meeting elected as a minister within the government, but he gave quite a robust speech and if I draw your attention to some sections of that. "Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation? I say this with a reason and I must instantly add that knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people, I do not hesitate in selecting the first option, the option of war, because I believe that the fate, our fate, the fate of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the fate of the Serbs in BH cannot be solved in any other way but by war." And later on at the bottom he says, "Why do I say that the option of war seems more likely to me? Because only what has been conquered militarily may become really and truly ours." He also continued in his speech and made some references that certain facilities should either be captured or destroyed, including the radio and TV stations, he makes reference to that on page 24, and he also discussed the fact that certain military facilities had been handed back or were no longer in their control and he even made a reference that -- to the military hospital in Sarajevo, that if the military hospital was to end up in the hands of the enemy, that he was for the destruction of that hospital. So that the enemy had nowhere to go for medical help. So he in essence advocated a very robust view that the war option was what was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, very briefly, I think we should cover this quickly, on page 29, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin gives his views. Did he -- can you tell us what his view was and whether he agreed with the war option or negotiation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, according to the minutes of the meeting, Mr. Brdjanin in his introduction to his comments gave a hearty bravo to Mr. Kalinic and stated himself, although he seems quiet when I see -- when I seem hawkish, his opinions are the closest to mine. Mr. Brdjanin then went on to discuss a number of -- speak about a number of other issues. The first one was the general issue of loyalty and whether Muslims could hold certain positions and he also made specific reference to a Muslim teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps, which was presumably making reference to Mesud Hasotic, who was the assistant commander for morale in the corps. He also discussed the issue of the linkage between the Serb area in Croatia, the SAO in Krajina, and argued that they should have establish communication links, information links, and create all the prerogatives necessary for linking those states. And I would draw you back to what Mr. Karadzic said in relation to the -- his articulation of why the corridor was important because the corridor enabled the Bosnian Serb areas in Bosnia and the Bosnian Serb areas in Croatia to link up with Serbia, and I would argue that Mr. Brdjanin here is saying we must improve our links with the SAO in Krajina and in essence look forward to having all Serbs in one state. So he's advocating that that process should start immediately. He advocates full mobilisation, and also makes comments at the end of his speech that in essence as few weapons should leave the Krajina or the RS territory and go back to Serbia, presumably referring to the transition of the JNA into the VRS, that they should keep hold of as many of the weapons that they -- that the JNA had. So those were some of the themes of Mr. Brdjanin's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who was the highest military official at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: General Mladic was at the meeting and was appointed as the new Commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you go through what you think, if there are any, the significant -- his view on what's being discussed there, the war option, the methods of achieving the six strategic objectives? He begins speaking on page 37, which is 0091-3537.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: General Mladic gives a rather long speech which is not always the easiest one to follow. But in essence gives his view of military issues, but in certain sections, does appear to utter some words of caution. I would argue from his -- some of his comments he's clear he is acutely aware of this issue of resettlement and potentially from a military perspective is more acutely aware of what that may in essence entail and he does utter a few words of caution. If I draw your attention to page 39, and the section, he says: "People and peoples are not pawns, nor are they keys in one's pocket that can be shifted from here to there. It is something easily said but difficult to achieve." And later, in on page 41, he makes reference in fact to Colonel Hasotic and that in essence it's from a soldier's perspective better to have someone like him in the trenches fighting with him than on the other side. But I draw your attention to the section where he says: "Therefore we cannot cleanse nor can we have a sieve to sift so that only Serbs would stay or that only Serbs would fall through and the rest leave." Well, that is -- that will not -- I do not know how Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic would explain this to the world. People -- that would be genocide. And a bit further down he says: "This does not mean that Muslims have to be expelled or drowned." And from those quotes, I believe that General Mladic is aware of what is being discussed and what separation from the other two communities in fact means. That said, he does later on in the report, well, primarily he accepts the position as commander of the VRS a position which he remains in through the whole of the war, and later on in the -- in his speech, he does make mention that what was being discussed should be guarded as their closest secret. And that is referenced in my report on footnote 65 on page 27. "Let us not put our minds into what we are doing but let us also think thoroughly about it and let us be cautious about when to keep mum. No, this thing we are doing needs to be guarded as our deepest secret. And what our representatives appearing in the media, political talks, and negotiations are going to say and they do into the to present our goals in a way that will sound appealing to" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. "And they do need to present our goals in a way that will sound appealing to the ears of those we want to win over to our side without being detrimental to our Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can break for one minute, for the record that is on page 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please continue. I'm sorry I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No. Those are the comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Finally, in a way sort of summing up some of what's been going on and what we have been talking about, in paragraph 1.54 of your report, which is on page 29. Have you found that page?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You state: "By the summer of 1992, it was clear that the objectives of creating a Serb state and separating the communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were not just political rhetoric but were a driving factor behind the actions of the military." Do you stand by that statement or do you have any additional explanation or qualification you'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No. I stand by that, and I would argue that the events as they panned out would appear to indicate that that was the case. I've already highlighted the issues of the corridor and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything else you think should be mentioned about the 16th assembly session before we move on? I don't want to leave out anything you might find important.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No, think those are the main key issues that I derive from the minutes of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a few minutes early, Your Honour, but I'm about to move to another chapter, so it might make sense to stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a -- can we settle for a 20-minute break today instead of 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's fine with you, but I don't know if it is fine with Mr. Ackerman and the rest?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know if I agree to that, the first thing that will happen is the interpreters will tell me that they have a contract and that I should not agree. I'll agree and take that heat, but I know their contract calls for a minimum of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Interpreters? Engineers? They are consulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Don't want to start a strike, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, what I'd like to do now is go through some of the documents you selected in the same area of your report which reflect actions taken after the 16th assembly meeting. The first one I'd like to look at is footnoted in your report as footnote 77. That's on page 29 of your report. And that should be a memo from the 1st Partisan Brigade outlining the minutes of a meeting. That has been previously exhibited as P51. Now, you cited this in your report as an example of how the strategic goals adopted or outlined at the assembly meeting we've been discussing were disseminated as was the announcement of the creation of the VRS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if it's possible for me just to add something very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. If at any time if you want to add something, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope I don't say that the 16th assembly session in itself, if you like, was a start point for issues, I also include military related issues. There were military activity, there was significant military activity in areas well before the 16th assembly session. I find difficult to somehow explain exactly clearly the 16th assembly session sometimes, but there was activity prior to that and I wouldn't want it to be conveyed that this if you like was the start point of activity both in a military perspective and in other areas. In relation to this document, this comes two days after the 12th -- 16th assembly session and I think from certain aspects of the document, it's clear that people are very aware of the discussions at that assembly session. If you take you to the agenda first to start with, assessment of the political and military situation in the municipalities, function and conduct of government bodies, instructions on the meeting itself on the 12th of May, and on the founding assembly of the Serbian Krajina and the founding of the army and discussions and suggestions and further cooperation with JNA units in regard to securing territory and the treatment of combatants in the region of the Serbian Krajina. Those who attended the meeting, Colonel Stanislav Galic, who was commander of the 30th Partisan division, a subordinate of General Talic; Colonel Branko Basara, who is brigade commander at that time located in Sanski Most; and a number of the municipal presidents from the area that the 30th division covered, and the minutes of this meeting discussed those issues on the agenda. And in particular, if I can draw your attention to page 3, and the comments by Milan Malidza, the President of the Mrkonjic Grad municipality assembly, again a municipality in the 30th division zone, he makes mention of the fact that the armed forces of the Krajina would be called the army of the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later in the year renamed the VRS. He states: "It was assessed that the army was capable of conquering a lot of territory," and he outlines the strategic goals set at the Banja Luka meeting and he notes those on page 4. There are some slight differences in his articulation of the goals than were articulated by Mr. Karadzic, but in essence they are the same six strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you look at page 4 of the document, at the bottom, above the bullet points, we see that Colonel Galic has made some suggestions, and the first one is that: "The conclusions of the meetings in Banja Luka are to be implemented and will also be forwarded to the commands of units and municipalities." Can you just tell us what significance that has to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that question is answered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness didn't mean to do this but he's referring to what Milan Malidza said and he says that Malidza said the army could conquer a large territory, and in fact that is not what he said. He said the army could occupy a large territory, and those are two very different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Would you take Mr. Ackerman's point or would you like to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tragically can't speak B/C/S, Your Honour, and I would defer to somebody who can. The translation I have says "conquer." If it's "occupy," then I would accept that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have the wrong translation again, Your Honour. The one I have says that the army can occupy a large territory. If his says "conquer," I apologise to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed and then we'll clarify this later. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you remember the question, can I -- I can repeat it. I was directing you to page 4, Colonel Galic's suggestion that: "The conclusions of the Banja Luka meeting the 16th assembly be implemented and forwarded to the commands of units and municipalities." Can you tell me what significance that has to you if any.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's self-evident that Colonel Galic is expecting that those decisions and discussions at Banja Luka were to be passed down both the military chain, to units, and presumably soldiers within those units, and also down through the municipality and civilian chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think I said the date of this document on the record. It's 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's stated in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness in the beginning said two days after the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We pay attention, Mr. Nicholls, usually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One other issue in relation to that. The final comment is that it was suggested that future meetings of this kind be held every 15 days and that the presidents of the municipal assemblies were responsible for preparing those meetings. This I think is important in relation to the link between the military and civilian organisations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look at the next footnote you have cited, that is footnote 78, also on page 29 of your report, this has previously been exhibited, it's P1597. And this is a 21st of May, 1992, 1st Krajina Corps command mobilisation order. Could you tell us why you selected this document and what relevance it has so that you cited it in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: There are a few sections in this document I'd like to draw your attention to. The first one is the date. This comes immediately after the technical withdrawal of the JNA from the VRS. And it's a call for mobilisation, general mobilisation of the army which of course had been called for at the 16th assembly session by a number of delegates, including Mr. Brdjanin and others. The first paragraph makes comment of a decision of the Serbian republic BH Presidency of the previous day on the 20th of May which had initiated the mobilisation of all citizens. And the document describes what, in fact, that means. And I'd like to just draw your attention to a number of sections, section 1 on page 2 of the translation, General Talic says: "Immediately establish direct contact with municipal and military and territorial organs on the ground offering expert and material support for the mobilisation process." Point 6, explain to conscripts as they arrive the goals of our struggle and brief them on their duties and rights. This again would seem to echo the comment that Galic had made in that meeting we've just discussed and also the goals that were being discussed in the 12th of May. And point 8: "Until the units receive concrete combat tasks engage them in the following tasks." And if I draw your attention to point 4: "Establish the closest possible cooperation with the people and legal authorities within their zones of responsibility." And this document was to be disseminated or was disseminated from the address block to the units of the corps. So it establishes mobilisation, echoed from the 16th assembly session and it highlights in a number of areas the need to have this cooperation with authorities on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. There is another order from the same date, 21st of May, which is interesting. It's cited, it's footnote 79 in your report. This is P58. I'd like you to just take a moment and again highlight the points that you find most relevant in this report about the actions which the military has taken in this period in May, and if you could also tell us who Mr. Vukelic, the author is, and what his function within the corps was.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report, rather than an order, I think, written by Colonel Milutin Vukelic who was the assistant commander for morale and legal affairs in the corps. One of the key assistants or staff assistants of General Talic. One of his functions was to by the nature of his job to report on issues of morale, and including -- as a part of that job included disseminating, if you like, the political and security sort of situation as it was viewed by the corps to the units of the corps. And I believe this report is one of those type of reports that he would write relatively frequently, making it aware to the units of the corps the political and military situation. And it's dated again on the 21st of May, so the same day as the mobilisation instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, we've heard evidence already on who he was on who this gentleman and what his office involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted that explanation because the nature of this report it makes clear why it is written the way it has been and who it was -- that it was distributed to all units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just highlight, then, the points that you find relevant, Mr. Brown? I think we start on page 2.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. If I draw your attention to the first paragraph or components of the first paragraph on page 2, Colonel Vukelic states: "The constituent Serbian people who live on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina must struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples and form their own state. Only after that will they be able to decide with whom and how they will unite and associate." Paragraph 3: "To prevent the militant and criminal Muslim and Croatian anti-Serbian coalition and its paramilitaries from achieving their plans, the Serbian -- the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina are prepared and able to resist them by all means including armed struggle. That is why following the proclamation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of BH and the constituting of its state organs, the army of the Serbian Republic of BH was formed as the armed force of the Serbian people." Later on, in that same page: "The army of the Serb Republic of BH is the army of the Serbian people, of all patriots as well as of all citizens who are ready to fight in its ranks for the just goals of the Serbian people. The defence of the territorial integrity of the republic and peace in these areas." And he also says that: "The army is increasingly -- becoming an increasingly powerful guarantee of the survival of the Serbian people and their state and peaceful development." Also, if I can draw your attention to page 3 and a couple of sections there: "Special attention must be devoted to the broadest possible daily cooperation with the people and the development of the fullest possible mutual trust and respect. The Serbian people must continuously affirm their trust in the army which is now more of an army of the people than ever before." And just latterly at the end: "Inform all members of the army of the Serbian Republic of BH about the contents of this report in the most suitable way." So this document I believe is outlining from the corps what they believe are the reasons why they are about to engage in combat activity and importantly that this is to be disseminated down to the units of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think the point is clear but this also, does it not, reflect the convergence which we started off talking about.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Another document related to this section of your report is P385, which is contained in footnote 81 of your report, still on the same page, 29. This document has a number of interesting sessions -- sections, excuse me, and again highlights some of the goals which we talked about earlier. Could you just point us to what you think are the important sections of this document and why you selected it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document summarising, as the title states, combat morale for the month of May, so in essence summarising what had happened in May. I believe this document was signed by General Talic. If I draw your attention to a couple of sections in the very first paragraph, bearing in mind this was dated the 14th of June, "the entire zone of responsibilities is under -- is fully under control. There have been no incidents of combat positions being lost to the enemy. On the contrary we have taken new ones. We have operated successfully in crisis area such as Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kozarac, and Donji Vakuf." On page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. If I could stop you for one second then. So that is -- you characterise that as now, on the 21st -- on the 14th of June, a positive assessment of what's taken place since the mobilisation in May?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: In part 2, draw your attention to the paragraph that states: "The complex political and security situation in BH in May escalated into numerous armed conflict in a large number of towns in the Bosnian Krajina autonomous region, Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and the Jajce areas and beyond, Donji Vakuf, Travnik and Derventa areas. All these conflicts were organised by the BH TO and in conjunction with the Republic of Croatia and were imposed upon the Serbian people. Thanks to our realistic assessment and the engagement of the corps units, the armed conflicts have been solved in the best possible away and all the hot beds are under control." Later on, General Talic writes it's in our -- "it is our estimate a certain degree of chaos on total inter-ethnic war has been forestalled. This is confirmed by the continuously stable conditions in Banja Luka and many other towns as well as by the way in which control has been established in Kotor Varos, where a real explosion of armed conflict was threatening to erupt." If I move to page 3, there is a comment General Talic indicates: "Notwithstanding the positive tendencies in the Bosnian Krajina autonomous region, its leadership in its public statements and concrete political actions maintains an independent attitude towards the Serbian Republic of BH government and there are attempts to interfere in commanding the corps and in some of its structures. As soon as we challenge certain officials on these points, they immediately state that the army needs to be cleansed of comeys, not infrequently some party leaders enlisting the help of certain reserve officers and soldiers attempt to secure an army of their own and thus profit from the war." I make reference to this in my report, that there were some difficulties reported in the military documents in terms of the relationship. I believe I come on to that later on. If I can highlight halfway down that same page: "The most difficult situation concerns the Muslim and Croat refugees in the area of the autonomous region, their security and the provision of food. The attempt to expel them to central Bosnia failed because of transportation difficulties and their resistance to leaving their places of residence. This is giving rise to vindictiveness and revenge and is resulting in the enemy closing its ranks." I believe this section is particularly important certainly in light of the comments at the 16th assembly session only a few weeks prior to this.
